title: High-Frequency Gravitational Wave Detection with Superconducting Qubits
authors: Heechan Yi, Seong Chan Park, Kyoungchul Kong, Myeonghun Park
abstract: High-frequency gravitational waves (HFGWs) provide a unique window into high-energy and early-universe physics, yet they evade traditional macroscopic interferometry. To bridge this detection gap, we propose a novel quantum-sensing paradigm utilizing superconducting transmon qubits embedded in resonant microwave cavities. Through the inverse Gertsenshtein effect, HFGWs propagating in a static magnetic field resonantly excite a cavity mode. By leveraging the characteristic spin-2 quadrupolar pattern of the induced electromagnetic field, we position qubits directly at the electric-field hot spots of the $\mathrm{TE}_{212}$ mode to act as localized sensors. Crucially, configuring this array as an entangled quantum register via symmetric Dicke states unlocks a fundamental scaling advantage: the signal probability scales quadratically with the qubit number, translating to a $h_{\min} \propto n_q^{-3/4}$ strain sensitivity scaling. We demonstrate that an idealized global register of 800 qubits reaches a strain sensitivity that surpasses standard macroscopic cavity-power limits by five orders of magnitude. Benchmarked against representative axion-haloscope parameters, this collective quantum enhancement decisively mitigates the profound Planck-scale suppression inherent to gravitational interactions, establishing a transformative framework for next-generation HFGW searches in the GHz band.
summary: The paper proposes using superconducting transmon qubits as highly sensitive detectors for high-frequency gravitational waves. By leveraging the inverse Gertsenshtein effect and encoding the signal into an entangled Dicke state register, they achieve a collective enhancement that dramatically improves strain sensitivity compared to classical limits. This establishes a transformative quantum framework for next-generation GW searches in the GHz band.
main_problem: Detecting high-frequency gravitational waves (HFGWs) which are too weak or oscillate at frequencies that evade traditional macroscopic interferometry methods.
main_result: The authors propose a quantum sensing framework where entanglement allows the strain sensitivity to scale as $h_{\min} \propto n_q^{-3/4}$, surpassing standard cavity limits by five orders of magnitude for 800 qubits.
method: They utilize the inverse Gertsenshtein effect, coupling HFGWs to superconducting transmon qubits embedded in microwave cavities, and enhance sensitivity using entangled Dicke states.
model_or_system: The system involves an array of superconducting transmon qubits acting as localized sensors within a resonant microwave cavity. The interaction is modeled via the effective four-current ($\mathbf{j}_{	ext{eff}}$) driven by the GW field, and the enhancement relies on mapping excitation parity using Dicke states.
key_observables: Strain sensitivity ($h_{\min}$), signal probability scaling ($\propto n^2$), and the characteristic spin-2 quadrupolar pattern of the induced electromagnetic field.
important_parameters: Qubit number ($n_q$), cavity quality factor ($Q$), operating frequency (GHz band), and the Planck-scale suppression inherent to gravitational interactions.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an idealized global entangled register, neglecting relaxation effects, and focuses on direct GW–EM coupling while using a monochromatic approximation for steady-state solutions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of incoming GWs relative to the cavity axis and show the effective current ($\mathbf{j}_{	ext{eff}}$) induced by different polarizations ($h_+, h_	imes$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem (HFGW detection gap), then details the quantum sensing mechanism involving the inverse Gertsenshtein effect at field hot spots, and finally derives the collective enhancement scaling using entangled Dicke states.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced concepts from cavity QED and many-body physics (Dicke states) to solve a fundamental problem in astrophysics/particle physics (GW detection), providing a concrete quantum advantage scaling law for experimental realization.
